# `nhms_synthetic.csv` — data dictionary

**Fully synthetic.** 5,000 simulated adults, generated by `data-raw/simulate_nhms_synthetic.py`
(seed `20261111`). The variable names and codings follow the NHMS-style extract used in the 2023
SBDR workshop so that the same narrative works, but **no row is a real person and no value is
derived from real survey records**. Risk gradients were chosen to look plausible for Malaysian
adults; they are *not* estimates of anything.

Why synthetic (and not the 2023 `nhms_dummy.csv`)? That file was built by scrambling each column
independently, which removes every relationship between variables — cross-validated AUC for all
three outcomes is 0.50. You cannot teach modelling on noise.

## Outcomes (binary, `1` = yes, `0` = no)

| Variable    | Meaning                                                              | Prevalence |
|-------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------:|
| `undx_dm`   | Undiagnosed type 2 diabetes (no known diagnosis, screening positive)  | 11.6 %     |
| `undx_hpt`  | Undiagnosed hypertension                                             | 23.3 %     |
| `undx_chol` | Undiagnosed hypercholesterolaemia                                    | 44.5 %     |
| `dm`, `hpt`, `chol` | *Known* diagnosis — all `0` by construction (sample = no known diagnosis). Zero-variance; `step_zv()` should drop them. | 0 % |

## Identifiers

| Variable | Meaning |
|----------|---------|
| `id`     | Row identifier 1–5000. **Not a predictor** — give it an `"id"` role in the recipe. |

## Sociodemographics

| Variable      | Coding |
|---------------|--------|
| `sex`         | 1 Female, 2 Male |
| `age`         | Years, 18–92 |
| `age_cat`     | 1 18–29, 2 30–39, 3 40–49, 4 50–59, 5 60+ (derived from `age`) |
| `ethnic`      | 1 Malay, 2 Chinese, 3 Indian, 4 Other Bumiputera, 5 Others |
| `residential` | 1 Rural, 2 Urban |
| `married`     | 1 Single, 2 Married, 3 Widowed/Divorced |
| `education`   | 1 None, 2 Primary, 3 Secondary, 4 Tertiary (0.8 % missing) |
| `income`      | Household income group — **note the odd coding kept from the original file:** 1 M40, 2 T20, 3 B40 |
| `hh_income`   | Monthly household income, RM |
| `occupation`  | 1 Government, 2 Private, 3 Self-employed, 4 Homemaker/unpaid, 5 Not working (student/retired/unemployed). ~16 % missing, more among the young, the old and homemakers (MAR). |

## Lifestyle

| Variable     | Coding |
|--------------|--------|
| `smoke`      | 1 Current, 2 Former, 3 Never |
| `alcohol`    | 1 Yes (current drinker), 2 No |
| `pa`         | 1 Physically active, 2 Inactive — **an exact recode of `pa_3cat`** (Inactive ⇔ Low). Use one or the other, not both, or linear models become rank-deficient. |
| `pa_3cat`    | IPAQ-style category: 1 Low, 2 Moderate, 3 High |
| `vig_day`, `vig_min` | Days/week and minutes/day of vigorous activity |
| `mod_day`, `mod_min` | Days/week and minutes/day of moderate activity |
| `walk_day`, `walk_min` | Days/week and minutes/day of walking |
| `mean_f`, `mean_v` | Mean servings/day of fruit and of vegetables |
| `cons_fv`    | 1 Adequate (≥ 5 servings/day), 2 Inadequate (derived) |
| `fam_hx_dm`  | Family history of diabetes: 1 Yes, 2 No (**new vs 2023 file**) |
| `fam_hx_hpt` | Family history of hypertension: 1 Yes, 2 No (**new**) |

## Anthropometry (≈ 7 % missing jointly; more among older and rural respondents — MAR)

| Variable  | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| `height`  | cm |
| `weight`  | kg |
| `bmi`     | kg/m² |
| `bmi_cat` | 1 < 25, 2 25–29.9, 3 ≥ 30 |
| `waist`   | Waist circumference, cm |

## Clinical measurements — **read this before modelling**

| Variable | Meaning | Sentinel |
|----------|---------|----------|
| `sys`, `dys` | Systolic / diastolic BP, mmHg | `-9` = not measured (4.6 %) |
| `rbs`    | Random blood sugar, mmol/L | `-9` = not measured (7.5 %) |
| `rchol`  | Random total cholesterol, mmol/L | `-9` = not measured (7.5 %) |

1. **Recode `-9` to `NA` first** (`dplyr::na_if()`), or your imputation and scaling will be wrong.
2. **These are target-leaking variables.** In NHMS an *undiagnosed* case is *defined* by this
   measurement: `undx_dm` is "no known diabetes **and** screening blood sugar above threshold".
   `rbs` therefore sits on both sides of the equation. A model that uses `rbs` to predict
   `undx_dm` gets AUC ≈ 0.98 and is useless as a screening tool, because by the time you have
   `rbs` you already have the answer. Same for `sys`/`dys` → `undx_hpt` and `rchol` → `undx_chol`.
   The workshop's "honest" predictor set is everything a community health volunteer could collect
   *without* a blood test or a BP cuff.

## Expected performance (5-fold CV AUC, for your reference — participants should discover this)

| Target     | Predictors            | Logistic | Random forest | XGBoost (tuned) |
|------------|-----------------------|---------:|--------------:|----------------:|
| `undx_dm`  | with `rbs` (leaky)    | 0.98     | 0.98          | 0.99            |
| `undx_dm`  | honest set            | 0.85     | 0.85          | 0.86            |
| `undx_hpt` | with `sys`/`dys`      | 0.99     | 0.98          | 0.99            |
| `undx_hpt` | honest set            | 0.82     | 0.82          | 0.83            |

The honest-set gaps between models are small *by design* — that is what tabular health data
usually looks like. The simulated truth contains several interactions and thresholds (family
history × obesity, sex-specific waist cut-offs, Indian ethnicity × overweight, post-menopausal
catch-up in women, young-obese bump), which is where tree ensembles and neural networks earn
their extra 0.01–0.02 AUC and what SHAP dependence plots should reveal.
